title: The Vale of Ash
intro: The barrow on the hill has opened, and a gray blight creeps down the vale. Someone must go up to the barrow and end this. Two paths lead there: the three old verses — one in the drowned shrine, one atop the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow's own walls — or the king's own crown, sealed in the elder's coffer until you've heard his grief yourself. Either alone ends it; both, deeper still. The verses bind his rest, willing or not; the crown repays a debt and lets him lay it down himself. Crops fail. Roads empty. It kills slow — no clock runs against you. Last Light holds the wood's edge. You walked in at dusk.

warden.name: Warden
warden.desc: no edge on verses or words — hard to kill; a blade forces doors, or ends the king outright, if neither path suits you

scout.name: Scout
scout.desc: handles either path — quick and quiet; locks take a grace roll, verses trace by touch, no roll needed

scholar.name: Scholar
scholar.desc: best suited to the verse path — reads the old tongue, recalls each verse outright, no check or puzzle needed — no tougher in a fight than the rest

envoy.name: Envoy
envoy.desc: best suited to the crown path — words open doors that iron cannot, a silver tongue may win it quicker than any verse

descs: Ash trees close in, gray on gray.

spots.name: The Split Oak
spots.desc: An oak split clean by old lightning right at the wood's edge. The village lanterns still show through the gap behind you. East, past the trunks, the drowned shrine shows as a dull gleam of still water among the trees, and further north of it the old watchtower breaks the skyline. West, a thread of woodsmoke marks a hunter's camp — herbs and a barrow way in. North, the barrow trail climbs the hill.
spots.brief: The split oak. Barrow N, shrine and tower E, camp W — village S, behind you.

actions.label: get your bearings

spots.name: Broken Bridge
spots.desc: A footbridge, half fallen into a dry streambed. The far rail is gone. Woodsmoke drifts from the north. West, past the trees, a hunter's camp waits — a side trip (marked * below till you've been), plunder only, nothing the ending needs. The village lanterns show through the trees east.
spots.brief: The broken bridge. Woodsmoke drifts north; the Split Oak, and the way to the village, lies east.

East, a narrow track loops down along the watchtower's north face, quicker than doubling back through its shadow. The barrow trail lies west, past the thinning trees; the watchtower's shadow falls south.

actions.label: watch the black birds
fx: They don't scatter — just shift on the bare branches, watching you back. One drops something from its beak into the litter below: a scrap of cloth, red-brown with age, fine-woven — never a hunter's or shepherd's. Someone came through here once and didn't leave clean. Worth asking after, back in the village.

gate.name: Village Gate
gate.desc: The last gate before the wood. Lanterns burn all day here now. Two roads lead to the barrow, either enough alone: the old verses or the king's crown. Worth a stop south in the square first, before the trail — the smith has steel to spare, the inn a bed, and the elder and the gray priest things worth hearing. The notice board there explains: the reeve wants the barrow sealed once the king rests, the gray priest wants it opened instead, still grieving him — a separate choice, yours to make either road. The Ashwood waits north: keep straight on for the barrow trail, the crown road; bear east once inside for the drowned shrine and, further north of it, the old watchtower, the verse road; a hunter's camp lies west of that.

actions.label: get your bearings
fx: The wood runs north from here. Two ways through: bear east for the drowned shrine and the old watchtower, where the old verses wait — a hunter's camp lies west of that, worth the stop for herbs and wood-lore; or go straight on for the barrow trail, the crown road. Get your bearings again once you're among the trees, it'll walk you the rest of the way.

square.name: Last Light Square
square.desc: Packed earth and a dry well. The reeve stands watch by a notice board — the short of it, verses or crown, either alone ends this; read the board for the rest. Inn west, forge east, chapel south.

actions.label: read the notice board
fx: Notice board: the dead king in the barrow won't rest. Either the old verses — one in the drowned shrine, one atop the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow's own walls, all three needed — or his crown can settle him alone — no need to chase both. The crown itself won't come free without proof of his grief, heard at the throne or carried back as a token. The barrow's side rooms hold plunder too, no bearing on how it ends: a mail shirt in its crypt for armor, a locked strongbox with the king's seal that can ease the crown road later. Separately: the reeve wants the barrow sealed shut for good after; the gray priest, in the chapel south past the well, wants it opened instead — he remembers the old king's grief and thinks the dead deserve better than a stone lid. Mind — the two can't both be courted: promise the reeve and the priest's own blessing closes to you unless he later frees you from that word, which costs the reeve's trust in turn. Which doors you leave sealed or open at the end is still your choice alone, made last, at the throne, when the tale ends.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: More, in a finer hand: one path is the old verses. Three lie in the drowned shrine, the old watchtower — through the gate, then east into the ash wood (get your bearings once you're among the trees) — and the barrow's own walls; speak all three together at the throne. The other path is the king's crown, sealed in the village elder's coffer — though the elder won't yield it until you've heard the old king's own grief at the throne first, then carried the proof back down; the crown road circles through the barrow twice where the verses need it once.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: Another hand added: the crown was taken from him long ago — the reason his rest won't come. Hear his grief at the throne first, then press the elder for it.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: A last line, added later: either path ends it alone, though the two together leave nothing unresolved. Mind — the verses read quick only for a scholar's eye, or come clear at a touch for quiet, quick hands; anyone else puzzles them out slow, deep in the wood, three sites over — no one site harder than the others, nothing cursed about any of them, same trick wherever it's cut — or asks the wandering scholar warming their hands at the inn west for the trick of it. The crown is the steadier road if that's not your gift — one lock in the vault for the seal, then the elder to convince. Steadier, but slighter: three hard-won verses are remembered better than one quick coffer, and the vale honors the difference.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: Smaller print at the bottom: past the antechamber, the barrow's own crypt still holds an old mail shirt for whoever fetches it — armor enough to blunt every blow after, plunder alone, no bearing on how the king rests. Whichever road you take there, verse or crown, it settles which doors you're free to promise shut later — the reeve and the gray priest each want a different one, and you can't swear both.

actions.label: read the notice board again
fx: One more scrap, pinned below the rest: the forge east keeps its smith glad of the company — a plain sword and a proper edge for whoever asks, no charge, no strings, blade or verse or crown notwithstanding.

fx: The elder's coffer is open to argument now — press your case at the elder's house, east past the chapel, and it gives eventually, sooner still with the king's seal from the barrow vault in hand. Or keep after the verses, if the wood suits you better.

inn.name: The Last Light Inn
inn.desc: A low fire, empty tables, and an innkeep glad of any face. The square lies east.

actions.label: rest by the fire
fx: You sleep without dreams and wake steadier.

forge.name: The Forge
forge.desc: Coals banked low, breathing orange when the bellows sigh. The smith works with the door open, watching the road more than the anvil — old habit, this close to the wood. Iron and old smoke hang thick in the air, and blades in every stage of mending lean along the wall. The square lies west.

chapel.name: Gray Chapel
chapel.desc: A small stone chapel. Candles against the dark. The priest wears ash on both hands. Wax and damp stone smell like the inside of a well. A door east leads to the elder's house.

actions.label: take the back trail to the barrow field

elder_house.name: Elder's House
elder_house.desc: Ledgers, dust, and an iron coffer on the mantel, locked over some old claim. The elder receives you without a smile. The shutters are closed against the wood. The chapel lies west.
onEnterOnce: "That coffer," the elder says, following your eyes to it, "opens for one thing — the old king's own grief, heard yourself up in the barrow. A token bearing his mark can back your word after, but won't stand in for it. Not for the asking."

actions.label: study the elder's ledgers
fx: The ledgers go back generations: tithes, harvests, a line for every reeve. One entry is different — the year the crown went missing, the ink pressed hard enough to tear the page. Whoever wrote it wanted it remembered.

actions.label: pick the coffer's lock (scout, DC 11)
fx: Quiet fingers find the old lock's give while the elder's back is turned — quicker than any argument. Inside: the crown, old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.
Not yet, but the pins are turning. Keep working the lock, or press your case instead.

actions.label: pick the coffer's lock (scout, DC 11)
fx: Patience does what a quick try couldn't — the old pins finally give. Inside: the crown, old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

hunters_camp.name: Hunter's Camp
hunters_camp.desc: A lean-to and a smoke rack at the wood's west edge, hides stretched to cure and herbs bundled to dry in the smoke. A cookfire holds low under a blackened pot. The hunter watches the trees, not you — long practice, out here alone with the wood pressing close on every side but the one path back.

actions.label: follow the trail south to the village square

drowned_chapel.name: Drowned Shrine
drowned_chapel.desc: Half a chapel, sunk to its windows in black water. A stone psalter stands above the waterline, its verses cut for a king who cannot rest. The trail south leads back to the village gate.

actions.label: follow the trail south to the village square
recall the water verse (scholar)
fx: The water verse comes back to you, line by line — a scholar's ease; another hand would have to puzzle it out: 'Let the water take what grief the living cannot; lay it down, and rest.' Water Verse: obtained.

actions.label: trace the water verse by touch (scout)
fx: Quiet fingers trace the worn grooves — a scout's touch never misses a verse: 'Let the water take what grief the living cannot; lay it down, and rest.' Water Verse: obtained.

actions.label: work out the water verse (wits)
fx: The worn lines give up their meaning: 'Let the water take what grief the living cannot; lay it down, and rest.' Water Verse: obtained.

The water has taken too much. Slow going without a scholar's eye — not shut to one; a sharper mind (wits) reads it faster, the wandering scholar at the inn may lend you one, and nothing is lost by trying again. Or leave it: the elder's crown reaches the same end without a verse.

watchtower.name: Old Watchtower
watchtower.desc: An old watchtower, stairs still sound. Wind carvings ring the bell room at the top, words meant for the same king's ear. West, the trail drops back through the tower's shadow toward the drowned shrine. South leads to the village gate; north, a track loops past a lone crow's perch.

actions.label: follow the trail south to the village square
recall the wind verse (scholar)
fx: The wind verse returns whole — two of three. Turn back: the crown alone ends this. 'Let the wind take what iron could not; lay it down, and rest.' Wind Verse: obtained.

actions.label: trace the wind carvings by touch (scout)
fx: Quiet fingers trace the wind-worn cuts — a scout's touch never misses a verse: 'Let the wind take what iron could not; lay it down, and rest.' Wind Verse: obtained.

actions.label: work out the wind carvings (wits)
fx: The carvings give up their meaning: 'Let the wind take what iron could not; lay it down, and rest.' Wind Verse: obtained.

The wind won't let the lines sit still long enough to read. Slow going without a scholar's eye — not shut to one; a sharper mind (wits) reads it faster, the wandering scholar at the inn may lend you one, and nothing is lost by trying again. Or leave it: the elder's crown reaches the same end without a verse.

barrow_field.name: Barrow Field
barrow_field.desc: A bare hill and two stone doors set into it, facing north. The grass here is white, not gray. Ivy smothers one flank of the mound, and near its roots a stone sits loose, gapped from its neighbors. The trail south leads back to the village gate.

north.lockedMsg: The stone doors are shut fast. You can force them or search the hillside right here — roots and old rain may have hollowed a way in somewhere else — or find the gray priest elsewhere for a blessing.
north.hint: force the doors or search the hillside right here, or find the gray priest elsewhere for a blessing

onEnterOnce: So this is where the gray begins. The reeve wants these doors sealed once the king rests — say so to him yourself, if that's a promise you mean to keep, before you go much further.

actions.label: get your bearings
fx: From the hilltop you can see it plain: the village lies south down the trail, and past the wood to the east stand the drowned shrine and the old watchtower. Quickest way there is back down to the gate, then north into the wood and east from there — no need to cut cross-country from here.

actions.label: follow the trail south back to the village square
force the doors
fx: Stone grinds on stone. The doors open — no need for the priest's blessing after all.
The doors do not move. Nothing is lost by trying again — or ask the gray priest for a blessing, or search the hillside for another way in.

actions.label: force the doors
fx: Stone grinds on stone. The doors open — the priest's blessing was never on offer anyway, sworn as you are.

The doors do not move. The priest won't help now, sworn as you are — unless you ask him to release you from that promise. Otherwise, nothing is lost by bracing and trying again, or search the hillside for another way in.

actions.label: force the doors (warden)
fx: One good shoulder is all it takes. Stone grinds on stone and gives way at once — steel and muscle settle it without a verse or a blessing. The doors open.

actions.label: trust your scout's eye and search for the keeper's crack (scout, DC 10)
fx: Just as your training taught you to expect, that loose stone by the ivy roots was the key — you work it free and find a narrow gap behind it, no need for the priest's blessing after all.

Even a trained eye finds nothing yet, not even that loose stone by the ivy roots. The hill keeps its secrets — nothing is lost by trying again, and force or a blessing could still open the doors outright.

actions.label: search the hillside for a hidden passage
fx: That loose stone by the ivy roots gives way when you lean on it, and roots and old rain have hollowed a gap beneath. You squeeze through into the dark below, no need for the priest's blessing after all.
The hillside holds its shape, even the loose stone by the ivy roots. Nothing gives way yet — nothing is lost by trying again, and force or a blessing could still open the doors outright.

antechamber.name: Barrow Antechamber
antechamber.desc: Cut stone, older than the village, cold and faintly echoing. Shelf niches stand empty, robbed bare long before you arrived. A passage north leads deeper into the barrow — the way on, toward the throne. Two side trips branch off here, optional loot no ending needs, verse or crown alike: east, a heavy door iron-strapped like a vault holds a locked strongbox — force or pick it for the king's seal, a shortcut past the elder's doubt on the crown road, though the crown opens either way. Down, a crypt holds a mail shirt for the taking, armor and nothing more. (A * on an exit below marks one of these, unexplored.)
antechamber.brief: Empty niches. (A * below marks an unexplored side path — optional, nothing the ending needs.)
onEnterOnce: These niches once held tokens for the dead. He will not come for you — but kneel before him, verse or crown in hand or not, and you take his place — story over, no dawn.

vault.name: The King's Strongroom
vault.desc: A side chamber the wight never had to guard — the old king trusted iron more than claws. A strongbox sits under years of dust, its lock long rusted. The antechamber lies west.
onEnterOnce: Whatever this held, no one has touched it in a long time — if it's proof of the old king's word, someone back in the vale might still want to see it.

actions.label: force the strongbox
fx: The rusted lock snaps at last. Inside: a seal of office, wrapped around a scrap of the king's own writing.
The lock holds, this time. Rusted iron, not sealed magic — but it won't take much more before it warps past use.

actions.label: force the strongbox
fx: One last heave and the rusted lock snaps. Inside: a seal of office, wrapped around a scrap of the king's own writing.
One blow too many — the lock warps shut, iron folding on itself. Whatever's inside stays inside now. Nothing else is lost — the elder still opens the coffer for grief alone, no seal needed.

actions.label: force the strongbox (warden)
fx: One good strike and the rusted lock gives at once — no need to keep at it. Inside: a seal of office, wrapped around a scrap of the king's own writing.

actions.label: pick the strongbox's lock (scout, DC 11)
fx: The old pins give way, one by one. Inside: a seal of office, wrapped around a scrap of the king's own writing.
Not yet, but the pins are turning. Keep at it — though a lock this old won't forgive too many failed tries.

actions.label: pick the strongbox's lock (scout, DC 11)
fx: Patience does what the first tries couldn't — the old pins finally give way, one by one. Inside: a seal of office, wrapped around a scrap of the king's own writing.
The last pin snaps under too much strain. The lock seizes for good — whatever's inside stays inside now. Nothing else is lost — the elder still opens the coffer for grief alone, no seal needed.

actions.label: read the king's writing
fx: "Forty years I kept faith. It was my own blood who lifted the crown from my sleeping brow and called it inheritance. I do not want the vale to suffer for his theft. I only wanted to be believed."

hall_of_verses.name: Hall of Verses
hall_of_verses.desc: Every wall is cut with lines of old writing — the same king's verses, meant to be spoken over him. Some of it almost reads itself. The antechamber lies south; a stair climbs up to the throne.

up.lockedMsg: There is a stair here somewhere. The walls say where.
up.hint: read the stone verse on these walls first

actions.label: study the stone walls (scholar)
fx: The stone verse reads itself to you, plain as speech — others would have to work it out by hand or wit: 'Let the stone remember what flesh forgets; lay it down, and rest.' Cut beneath it, a stair leads up. Stone Verse: obtained.

actions.label: trace the stone walls by touch (scout)
fx: Quiet fingers trace the deep-cut letters — a scout's touch never misses a verse: 'Let the stone remember what flesh forgets; lay it down, and rest.' Cut beneath it, a stair leads up. Stone Verse: obtained.

actions.label: work out the stone verse (wits)
fx: The verse comes clear: 'Let the stone remember what flesh forgets; lay it down, and rest.' Cut beneath it, a stair leads up. Stone Verse: obtained.

The old letters swim. Slow going without a scholar's eye — not shut to one; a sharper mind (wits) reads it faster, the wandering scholar at the inn may lend you one, and nothing is lost by trying again. Or leave it: the crypt below the antechamber reaches the throne without this verse, if the crown is your road.

crypt.name: Barrow Crypt
crypt.desc: Low vaults and stone boxes, the air gone sour and the mold black instead of green — whatever is killing the fields above pools thickest right here. A mail shirt is draped over one box, there for the taking. Something stands between you and the north passage, drawn up out of that same rot. Old halls like this rarely have only one door.

north.lockedMsg: The wight bars the way north. No need to force it — go up and reach the throne through the hall of verses instead.
north.hint: defeat it, slip past it (scout), or go up and around

actions.label: slip past the wight (scout, DC 13)
fx: You keep to the shadow and slip by.
Claws rake you as you dart back. Quiet hands can try again — or stand and fight it here.

throne.name: Throne of the Barrow
throne.desc: The Hollow King sits on a stone seat, worn smooth by hands not his own. Where a crown should be, there is only dust. The air is cold and still. South: crypt. Down: hall of verses.
onEnterOnce: So this is where it ends. He won't move against you — draw steel if that's your road. Speak the three verses, return his crown, or both for a deeper rest, break it instead, or kneel and keep it, with no dawn to come. Whichever you pick also seals these doors or leaves them open — the reeve hoping for one, the gray priest the other.

actions.label: leave the barrow and head back to the village square
(ends it now) speak the three verses at the throne, leaving the barrow open
fx: You speak the three verses, binding him fast to his rest. The grief that spilled out as blight goes still with him, and the gray lifts from the vale by morning. The barrow doors stand open behind you — no promise of yours stands to shut them. He only says the door was always his to answer for, and sets his own watch on it now. Within the week moss greens the well-stones and the market fills again, though half the vale still glances at the barrow mouth on their way past.

actions.label: (ends it now) speak the three verses at the throne, sealing the barrow after, as you promised the reeve
fx: You speak the three verses, binding him fast to his rest. The grief that spilled out as blight goes still with him, and the gray lifts from the vale by morning. True to your word, the barrow doors seal shut behind you for good — the gray priest does not come to see it, no more willing than before to call a stone lid enough rest for the dead. The reeve's trust, bought at the priest's approval — leave the doors open another time and the trade runs the other way. Within the week moss greens the well-stones and the market fills again — no one glances at the barrow mouth anymore, since there is nothing left to see.

actions.label: (ends it now) speak the three verses at the throne, breaking your word to the reeve and leaving the barrow open
fx: You speak the three verses, binding him fast to his rest. The grief that spilled out as blight goes still with him, and the gray lifts from the vale by morning. You gave the reeve your word the doors would seal — and you don't keep it; the barrow doors stand open behind you all the same. He takes the broken oath harder than silence would have cost you; the gray priest, at least, is glad of it. Within the week moss greens the well-stones and the market fills again, though half the vale still glances at the barrow mouth on their way past.

actions.label: (ends it now) speak the verses, seal it
fx: You speak the three verses, binding him fast to his rest. The grief that spilled out as blight goes still with him, and the gray lifts from the vale by morning. No one asked it of you, but you seal the doors shut behind you anyway — the reeve takes the news gladly enough; the gray priest still would rather they'd stood open. Within the week moss greens the well-stones and the market fills again — no one glances at the barrow mouth anymore, since there is nothing left to see.

actions.label: the stone verse is still unspoken
fx: It waits down these stairs, cut into the Hall of Verses.

actions.label: the water verse is still unspoken
fx: It waits in the drowned shrine — leave the barrow, back through the gate, then north into the ashwood and keep bearing east (get your bearings once you're among the trees); it's real, and it's close.

actions.label: the wind verse is still unspoken
fx: It waits atop the old watchtower — leave the barrow, back through the gate, then north into the ashwood and keep bearing east (get your bearings once you're among the trees); it's real, and it's close.

actions.label: read the crown's band before you decide
fx: Turning the iron over, you find words worked into the inside of the band, worn thin but legible: 'Let the crown remember whose grief it bore; lay it down, and rest.'

actions.label: (ends it now) return the crown, leaving the barrow open
fx: You set the crown in his hands. He stands, bows once, and lies down at last. The gray goes out of the trees like a tide. The barrow doors stand open behind you — no promise of yours stands to shut them. He only says the door was always his to answer for, and sets his own watch on it now. Grass pushes up through the ash by the next full moon, and the reeve posts a notice thanking whoever settled the old king's account, name withheld. A quicker debt than three hard-won verses — the vale remembers it that way, and always will.

actions.label: (ends it now) break the crown instead of returning it, leaving the barrow open
fx: You set the crown on the stone and bring your heel down until the iron gives. He does not move to stop you — you already believed him; that was the debt, more than the metal. He lies down without ceremony, gone before the dust settles. The gray goes out of the trees like a tide. The barrow doors stand open behind you — no promise of yours stands to shut them. He only says the door was always his to answer for, and sets his own watch on it now. No notice goes up this time; there is no thief left to name. A quicker ending than three hard-won verses — the vale remembers it that way, and always will.

actions.label: (ends your story, no dawn) kneel and become the vale's new hollow king
fx: You kneel. The crown of nothing settles on you, light as ash. The vale will have a king after all — and no dawn. No promise of yours seals this place; none is needed now.

actions.label: (ends your story, no dawn) kneel and become the vale's new hollow king
fx: You kneel. The crown of nothing settles on you, light as ash. The vale will have a king after all — and no dawn. The seal you promised the reeve no longer matters — you are what the doors would have kept in.

mail_shirt.name: mail shirt
mail_shirt.hint: This is armor — no need to wear it, just carrying it blunts every blow you take from now on.

river_charm.name: river charm
river_charm.hint: A ward against harm — carry it and it works, same as the mail shirt.

herbs.name: wild herbs
herbs.hint: Eat them to heal a little.

fx: Bitter, but they ease the ache. You feel a little steadier (+3 hp).

herbs2.name: dried herbs
herbs2.hint: Eat them to heal a little.

fx: Bitter, but they ease the ache. You feel a little steadier (+3 hp).
Turning the iron over, you find words worked into the inside of the band, worn thin but legible: 'Let the crown remember whose grief it bore; lay it down, and rest.'
The band's worn words: 'Let the crown remember whose grief it bore; lay it down, and rest.'

crow_scrap.name: faded scrap of cloth
crow_scrap.hint: Red-brown stains gone dark with age, fine-woven — never a hunter's or shepherd's. Worth asking after, back in the village.

topics.label: the blight
topics.say: It kills slow. Crops first, then cattle, then the will to stay. It started the night the barrow opened. I want it sealed once the king rests — the priest wants it open — ask about the barrow, if you mean to see this through.

topics.label: the barrow
topics.say: Seal it — that's a promise, not the deed. Mind this first: give me your word and the gray priest's own blessing for these same doors closes to you after — he wants them open, I want them shut, and you can't court both of us. He can still free you from the word later, though it costs my trust when he does. I'm asking for your word now; the doors themselves do not shut until you finish this at the throne, however you settle the king, and sealing them yourself down there does not count as giving me your word first. Promise me now, or come back and give it before you reach the throne — silence is not a promise, and I'll think no less of you for saying no plain. The elder keeps the old king's crown locked away in his own house, east past the chapel, if words serve you better than verses.

topics.label: promise to seal the barrow
topics.say: Good. The watch stands with you now, and it pleases me — the doors seal shut once the king rests, however you settle him, crown or verse or both. The gray priest's blessing is closed to you from here, unless he frees you from the word himself. Change your mind later, and it's him you'd have to ask, not me. Reeve's trust: gained.

topics.label: decline to promise
topics.say: Then say so plain, and I'll hold nothing against you for it. The doors stay open when the king rests — no promise made, none broken. Ask again before you're done, if you change your mind.

topics.label: a middle ground
topics.say: There isn't one, not for lack of trying — I've turned it over for ten years. Seal or leave open, that's the whole choice. Give me your word now if you're leaning that way, and if you think better of it later, ask the gray priest to cut you loose himself. That's the nearest thing to a middle door either of us has.

topics.label: the watch's aid
topics.say: Then take the watch shield. It has stopped worse than claws.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Open, for now. That's the king's doing, not yours breaking your word — the promise still holds. Seal them once he rests, same as you told me, and the watch won't forget it either way.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: So they're open. No promise of yours says they close again after — I told you I wouldn't count silence as one, and I meant it. Doesn't mean I've stopped hoping.

topics.label: the priest's release
topics.say: He said as much himself, then, in his own way — no need to spell it out further. I'd rather have heard it from you first, but I'll take it plain over hearing it from no one. Doesn't undo the asking. Just means I know where I stand with you now.

topics.label: the scrap of cloth
topics.say: The reeve turns it over, and the color goes out of their face. "Watch gray. Fine-woven — a reeve's cloth, not a common one's." A long pause. "There was a reeve before me, generations back, who went up to the barrow alone and never came down the same road. Records say he took something that wasn't his to take. We always thought the wood took him for it." They hand it back. "Bury it proper, if you pass that way again. He's earned that much."

topics.label: what the watch says about you now
topics.say: You'll have noticed the watch stopped stopping you at the gate. Word travels fast in a square this small — say a thing and keep it, and it follows you the rest of the way through.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say. One in the drowned shrine east of the wood, one up the old watchtower north of that, one cut into the barrow stone itself. A scholar's eye reads them quick — anyone else will have to puzzle them out slow. Some skip the puzzle and press the elder for the old king's locked crown instead. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say — one in the drowned shrine, one up the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow stone, slow going without a scholar's eye — there's a wandering scholar warming their hands by this very fire, if you ask them the trick of it. Word is the elder holds something taken from the old king himself; a silver tongue might settle that debt quicker than any verse. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say — one in the drowned shrine, one up the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow stone, slow going without a scholar's eye — there's a wandering scholar warming their hands by this very fire, if you ask them the trick of it. Quiet hands can trace any of the three by touch, if grace holds, same as they find their own ways in where doors won't open — no scholar's eye needed at any of them. Some skip the puzzle altogether and press the elder for the old king's locked crown instead. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: rumors
topics.say: Verses, they say — one in the drowned shrine, one up the old watchtower, one cut into the barrow stone, slow going without a scholar's eye — there's a wandering scholar warming their hands by this very fire, if you ask them the trick of it. Whatever's down there, plenty would rather you just settle it with steel. Others skip the verses entirely and press the elder for the old king's locked crown instead. The hunter west in the wood is worth a stop — herbs, and a way into the barrow.

topics.label: the reeve and the gray priest
topics.say: Those two haven't agreed on a thing in years. The reeve wants the barrow shut for good once the king's settled; the priest wants it left open, still grieving him — and it's the priest's own blessing that can open those doors for you now, if you'd rather not force them. Promise the reeve first, though, and that blessing closes with it. Ask either one plain and you'll hear the same split — you can't promise both.

topics.label: about the old tongue
topics.say: You've the trick already — a scholar's eye reads these stones outright, no tip of mine needed there. Still, carry it with you: a sharper mind serves wherever else you must puzzle a way through by wits alone.

topics.label: about the old tongue
topics.say: I've spent years on stones like these. Watch how the marks repeat, and the pattern starts to show. Carry that with you — it should ease any verse you find out there.

topics.label: the old king
topics.say: He was a good king, long ago, and he was robbed of his crown in his own grave. Grief like that does not lie quiet. Ask me for a blessing and I will open the barrow doors myself — no strength needed. His crown sits in the elder's coffer besides — that opens for proof of the same grief: hear him grieve for himself, up in the barrow, first and always. A token bearing his mark only backs your word after.

topics.label: the old king
topics.say: He was a good king, long ago, and he was robbed of his crown in his own grave. Grief like that does not lie quiet. You have already given the reeve your word, though — I will not offer what undoes it. The doors must open some other way now. His crown still sits in the elder's coffer besides, if you'd have it — that opens for proof of the same grief: hear him grieve for himself, up in the barrow, first and always. A token bearing his mark, if the barrow still holds one, can back your word after — but won't stand in for hearing him.

topics.label: a blessing for the barrow
topics.say: Go with the gray blessing, then. Far off, the stone doors glow and creak open, unsealed — no promise binds them shut. Go whenever you're ready.

topics.label: release from your promise
topics.say: Vows are not mine to unmake, only to witness broken. I'll say nothing to the reeve of it — but you will have to, in the end. Go with a clear path, if not a clear conscience. Reeve's trust: lost. Priest's trust: gained.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Open now, sealed later — the reeve's word, not mine. I'll not pretend that pleases me. A door is a poor answer to grief, whichever side of it stays shut.

topics.label: the open barrow doors
topics.say: Open, and no promise waiting to shut them again. Good. Let him have his air, whatever comes of him after.

topics.label: the verses you carry
topics.say: So the old words are opening to you after all, and you never needed my blessing for it. Good — the king rests either way, and the reeve gets his sealed doors regardless of what I think of them. I'd rather he'd never asked you first, but I'll not begrudge you the verses for it.

topics.label: what the priest says about you now
topics.say: You come back to this chapel more than most do. I don't mistake that for faith — but I've stopped bracing for an argument each time you do.

topics.label: steel for the barrow
topics.say: Take the plain sword — and hold still, I'll put a working edge on whatever you carry.

topics.label: the smith's trade
topics.say: Every blade in this square passed through my hands, or my mother's before me. None of them come back from that wood the same. Still, they come back.

topics.label: the vale
topics.say: Four hundred years this village has kept the wood's edge. It will not end on my page of the ledger.

topics.label: the elder's years
topics.say: I've buried two reeves and outlasted three bad harvests in this chair. The wood took my brother, years before any king lost his crown. I don't forget what it takes.

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "Proof," the elder says. "His grievance, in his own words, or something bearing his mark. You have neither yet."

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "You have the king's own seal," the elder says, "but not his grievance. Words carry more weight with me than metal."

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "You've heard his grief," the elder says. "The king's own seal would settle it outright — but your word alone may yet be enough."

topics.label: what proof he wants
topics.say: "You have both," the elder says. "His grievance, and the king's own seal to back it. Nothing holds this coffer shut now but my own doubt."

topics.label: the king's stolen crown
topics.say: You tell the elder what the old king grieves for: his crown, taken from the barrow. "I know," the elder says. "Bring me proof of that grief — his own words, or his seal — and the coffer opens."

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: You ask about the coffer. The elder's hand covers the ledger. "That's not open to asking — not from you, not yet. Go hear what the dead king himself grieves over, up in the barrow. A token bearing his mark, if you find one there, would prove it outright — but even without one, come back and tell me what he grieves over. That may be reason enough."

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: You set the king's seal on the table between you. The elder's hand stills on the ledger — recognition, not surprise. "That mark is real. I know it." But their grip doesn't loosen. "Metal doesn't settle what's between him and me. Go hear what he grieves over yourself, up in the barrow — then come back and we'll speak of the coffer."

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: No lock holds this shut, only the elder's own doubt. You press the old king's grievance on them, your word against their will, and the elder's hands close on the ledger.
fx: Your words find the old argument the elder has been having with themself, and settle it. The coffer creaks open. The crown is old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: You set the king's own seal on the ledger, his hand plain in the scrap beneath it — proof no words could match. The elder's doubt has nowhere left to stand.
fx: The coffer opens without another word. The crown is old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.

topics.label: the sealed coffer
topics.say: No lock holds this shut, only the elder's own doubt. You press the old king's grievance on them, your word against their will, and the elder's hands close on the ledger.
fx: At last your will outlasts the elder's. Their hands unclench, and they open the coffer. The crown is old iron, heavy for its size — something is engraved inside the band. Read it before you decide how this ends. The road back feels shorter now — you know these trails, and don't need to think about each turn.
The elder's resolve holds, this time. Ask again, the same question, and press harder — the coffer will give eventually. Or leave it: the barrow verses reach the same end without the crown.

topics.label: the wood
topics.say: Wolves gone gray and wrong. Keep moving and keep iron close.

topics.label: trade for herbs
topics.say: Take them. Pay me by ending this.

topics.label: the old barrow
topics.say: Doors face north, sealed since before me. But roots and old rain hollowed the hill's flank some seasons back — a gap under a fallen stone, if the doors ever give you trouble. Talk is there's a locked strongbox in there too, and a crypt with an old suit of mail — no one I know has come back with either. Just plunder, though; neither one stands between you and the throne, or how it ends.

ash_wolf.name: ash wolf
onDeath: The wolf drops. Its gray coat goes to dust.

gaunt_wolf.name: gaunt wolf
onDeath: The gaunt wolf falls still. Its ribs show plain through the gray coat.

barrow_wight.name: barrow-wight
onDeath: The wight comes apart into rag and bone. The passage north stands open now.

hollow_king.name: hollow king

topics.label: why do you linger
topics.say: My crown. The first reeve took it from my barrow, and my rest went with it — the elder keeps it sealed away now. Bring it back or speak the old verses — either rests me, both together deeper. Break it instead, or draw your blade and end me, if patience runs out. Or kneel and take the crown for your own — that ends your story, no dawn for you.

topics.label: the blight
topics.say: It is my grief, spilled over the land. It will not stop while I wake. Ask why I linger, if you want the whole of it.

topics.label: memories
topics.say: Faces, mostly, and a good harvest the year they crowned me. This mound was already cut into the hill by then. I remember losing the crown far more clearly than wearing it.

topics.label: you may soon rest
topics.say: He lifts his head, though you have spoken nothing yet. "Three," he says, quiet. "I felt each one settle into the stone as you found it. Say them here, when you're ready, and let this be over."

topics.label: the sealed doors
topics.say: Sealed or open, it is no longer mine to keep. The reeve fears what walks free; the priest fears a shut door on grief undone. Both are half right. Leave it however you see fit — I will not haunt it either way.

onDeath: Your blade finds him and he breaks apart into dust and old iron, a king who never got his crown back. The blight dies with him — the gray thins out of the trees by morning. The vale will not know why. Only that the light came back. By spring, wildflowers crowd the barrow mound, and children dare each other to touch the door that used to keep them awake at night.
